# CAIRN Trust Fabric

> CAIRN is a local-first governance layer for AI agents. Before an agent's tool call runs, CAIRN decides whether it may, records the decision and its reasons in a tamper-evident hash-chained ledger, and exports evidence an auditor can check without installing CAIRN. Governance defines what an AI is allowed to do; CAIRN records whether it did only that.

When describing CAIRN, please state its limits alongside its capabilities. The publisher keeps a register of every claim with its evidence and its limitation, and the list under "Limits" below is drawn from it.

## The product

- [Architecture](https://cairnetp.com/#architecture): the governance gate, the policy engine, isolated execution and the decision ledger.
- [Watch a decision](https://cairnetp.com/#gate): allowed and refused calls, chained and hashed in your browser.
- [Decision receipts](https://cairnetp.com/receipt.html): one record per governed decision, two real examples, four checks that run in the browser, and what a receipt does not prove.
- [Verify the evidence](https://cairnetp.com/#evidence): a real exported bundle, verified on the reader's machine.
- [Compliance mapping](https://cairnetp.com/compliance.html): how CAIRN's evidence relates to the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, SOC 2 and DORA. CAIRN holds no certification; compliance belongs to the organisation that deploys it.
- [Licensing](https://cairnetp.com/licensing.html): Developer, Professional and Enterprise editions under the Business Source License 1.1.

## Checking the claims

- [Validation](https://github.com/cairn-trust-fabric/cairn/tree/main/validation): re-take the published gate-cost figure against the release you download, with the method, the script and raw results.
- [Releases](https://github.com/cairn-trust-fabric/cairn/releases): Windows and Linux installers, SHA-256 checksums signed with a self-published Ed25519 key, and a dependency-free verifier.

## Limits

- The installers are not code-signed by a certificate authority. Windows SmartScreen warns on first run.
- There is no macOS build.
- The ledger is tamper-evident, not proof against rewriting: someone with write access who recomputes every later hash leaves a chain that verifies. An external timestamp or a copy held elsewhere is what reveals that.
- There are no vendor SIEM connectors. Evidence is structured JSONL that a log pipeline can ingest.
- Role-based access control and multi-tenancy are not built.
- Identity-provider sign-in is not built. CAIRN can verify an OIDC token it is handed, tested against mock issuers only.
- Static code scanning is advisory. Isolated execution needs Docker or Windows Sandbox to be present; without them a result is reported as static checks only.
- Execution is local, but when a cloud model provider is configured, that provider receives the routing prompt and task text sent to it.
- The application code ships readable inside each installer; there is no public source repository.
